title: Breaking Down F4 Weaknesses | Sicilian Defence | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Against the early f-pawn thrust, the antidote is the immediate central break to d5 — and that's exactly why this move order isn't recommended; a genuine Grand Prix player would develop the knight first.
Don't recapture with the queen — instead develop the knight to f6, aiming to win the pawn back on your own terms rather than being dictated to.

The opponent defends the extra pawn, but that's no cause for alarm — the point is that the d4 square is now badly weakened. So switch into gambit mode: play e6, force the trade, and emerge with enormous compensation for the pawn. It's a well-known line every Sicilian player should carry.

The compensation, in one breath: huge central control anchored on d4, an enemy pawn stuck out like a sore thumb, a wretched bishop hemmed in behind its own pawns biting on granite, and an opponent's king with no safe haven, since the advanced pawn leaves castling short far from a cure. Spending a tempo on a rook-pawn move here is playing with fire when nothing is developed.
So develop with tempo — the bishop to d6, coming out with a hit on the weak pawn. Every developing move should also pose a threat when the opponent is this far behind.
The opponent ignores the threat, so simply grab the free pawn — it also unmasks a diagonal that can spell real trouble for the enemy king. Winning a pawn and opening a line in one is worth it.

Castle long for the adventurous game — the rook lands on the file already x-raying the queen and threatening a capture on c4, and above all it reinforces control of the key d4 square. Hold that square and everything is comfortable; now it's time to move in for the kill.

Don't rush the central knight jump — the move to reach for is the knight to g4, generating threats at the king with a capture on h2 looming and the knight eyeing an infiltration square. The storm clouds gather fast.

Here's the mating mechanism — the queen would mate on h2 but for the knight guarding it, and it can't leap over its own bishop. So distract the knight by planting a piece on d4 purely for tactics, not as an outpost; once it's captured, a bishop check on e3 forces the issue and the queen crashes into h2 for mate in two.

The opponent's better practical try was a pawn to g3 — though even that creates fresh kingside weaknesses, which a quick rook-pawn charge with h5 and h4 exploits, tearing the wing open for the attack. At least it would have been double-edged.

And a pretty resource to know: if the opponent forces a queen trade, ask the honest question — what if I just do it anyway? That yields the knight to d4, because after queens come off, a capture on the bishop forks the king and queen, winning the queen with an extra piece. The threats are simply too many to meet.
